lectures.title: Diabetes: epidemiology, classification, diagnosis & pathogenesis
key: Diabetes = chronic hyperglycaemia from defects of insulin secretion, action or both; > 537 million adults (IDF 2021); one of the 4 major NCDs with CVD, cancer, chronic respiratory disease
Diagnosis: FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL, 2-h OGTT (75 g) ≥ 200, HbA1c ≥ 6.5 %, or random ≥ 200 with symptoms; 2 abnormal results needed unless symptoms/crisis
Prediabetes: IFG 100 (ADA) / 110 (WHO)–125, IGT 140–199, HbA1c 5.7–6.4 % → lifestyle (DPP: −58 % progression), metformin in high-risk

Classes: T1D (autoimmune β-cell destruction, absolute deficiency), T2D (insulin resistance + progressive β-cell failure, 90 %), GDM, other specific types (MODY, pancreatic, endocrinopathies – Cushing, acromegaly, drugs – steroids)
T2D pathogenesis: ominous octet – ↓ insulin secretion, ↑ glucagon, ↑ hepatic glucose output, ↓ muscle uptake, ↑ lipolysis, ↓ incretin effect, ↑ renal reabsorption, brain
T1D: genetic (HLA DR3/DR4) + trigger (viruses) → insulitis; antibodies anti-GAD65, IA-2, ICA, insulin, ZnT8; honeymoon phase; associated autoimmunity (thyroid, coeliac, Addison)
Screening T2D: age ≥ 35 (ADA) or risk factors – overweight, first-degree relative, HT, dyslipidaemia, PCOS, GDM/macrosomia, acanthosis, CVD, inactivity; FINDRISC score
GDM: risk-based screening (course), 1st visit FPG/HbA1c for overt diabetes, 24–28 weeks 75 g OGTT (92 / 180 / 153 mg/dL); macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, later T2D in the mother
Initial assessment: HbA1c, lipids, creatinine/eGFR, UACR, liver tests, urinalysis (ketones), ECG, fundus (T2D), foot exam; C-peptide + antibodies if type uncertain
traps: HbA1c reflects 2–3 MONTHS, not weeks
Random glucose ≥ 200 is diagnostic ONLY with symptoms
Glucagon is INCREASED in T2D
Renal glucose reabsorption is INCREASED in T2D
LADA = adult, slow, but anti-GAD POSITIVE
Chronic complications at diagnosis point to T2D
gloss: impaired fasting glucose / impaired glucose tolerance
cleaved from proinsulin, marker of endogenous insulin
monogenic, autosomal dominant diabetes of the young (HNF1A, GCK)
oral glucose gives more insulin than IV glucose (GLP-1, GIP)

lectures.title: Acute & chronic complications: DKA, HHS, hypoglycaemia, micro- and macroangiopathy, foot
key: DKA: glucose > 250, pH < 7.3, HCO₃ < 18, ketones +, anion gap > 12; T1D (inaugural, missed insulin, infection), SGLT2i (euglycaemic DKA)
DKA treatment: 0.9 % saline → K⁺ (hold insulin if K < 3.3) → IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h → dextrose when glucose < 250 → SC overlap; bicarbonate only if pH < 6.9–7
HHS: elderly T2D, glucose > 600, effective osmolality > 320, pH > 7.3, no/minimal ketones, profound dehydration, coma; mortality 10–20 %
Hypoglycaemia: < 70 (L1), < 54 (L2), severe (L3); adrenergic + neuroglycopenic signs; Whipple triad; rule of 15; glucagon if unconscious; SU hypoglycaemia lasts – hospitalise
Microangiopathy pathways: polyol, AGEs, PKC, hexosamine → oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction
Retinopathy: NPDR (mild/moderate/severe 4-2-1) → PDR; macular oedema at any stage; laser, anti-VEGF; yearly fundus
Diabetic kidney disease: UACR (A1 < 30, A2 30–300, A3 > 300 mg/g) + eGFR; ACEi/ARB, SGLT2i, finerenone, BP < 130/80
Neuropathy: distal symmetric (monofilament, vibration, reflexes), autonomic (tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, ED), mononeuropathies; duloxetine/pregabalin, alpha-lipoic acid
Diabetic foot = neuropathy + ischaemia + infection; Wagner 0–5; off-loading, debridement, revascularisation; daily inspection, footwear
Macroangiopathy: CAD (silent ischaemia), stroke, PAD (ABI < 0.9; > 1.3 = calcified); CV disease is the main cause of death
traps: Total-body K is ALWAYS depleted in DKA even if serum K is high
Insulin IV in DKA, never SC first
Do not stop insulin when glucose normalises – add dextrose
Hypoglycaemic coma: sweaty, agitated, abrupt; DKA: dry, Kussmaul
Screen complications at T2D diagnosis but 5 years after T1D diagnosis
ACEi/ARB treat nephropathy, not retinopathy

lectures.title: Treatment: nutrition therapy, insulin, non-insulin drugs, targets & prevention
key: Targets: HbA1c < 7 % (individualise 6.5–8 %), fasting 80–130, post-prandial < 180 mg/dL, BP < 130/80, LDL by CV risk, no smoking, weight −5–10 %
Lifestyle: medical nutrition therapy (Mediterranean, low GI), ≥ 150 min/week activity + resistance, education (DSMES), psychosocial care
Metformin first line: ↓ hepatic glucose output; start 500–850 mg, max 2000–3000 mg; GI side effects, B12 deficit, lactic acidosis – stop if eGFR < 30, contrast/surgery
SGLT2i (gliflozins): glycosuria, weight ↓, BP ↓; HF and CKD protection regardless of HbA1c; genital mycosis, volume depletion, euglycaemic DKA
GLP-1 RA (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide SC; oral semaglutide): glucose-dependent insulin ↑, glucagon ↓, slow emptying, satiety; weight ↓↓, MACE ↓; nausea; no hypoglycaemia alone
DPP-4i (gliptins): weight-neutral, no hypo; sulfonylureas: cheap, potent, hypoglycaemia + weight gain; pioglitazone: insulin sensitiser, oedema, heart failure, fractures
Insulins: rapid analogues, regular (IV), NPH (cloudy), basal analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec), premixes; T1D basal-bolus 0.4–0.5 U/kg/day or pump/closed loop
Insulin in T2D: HbA1c > 10 % or glucose ≥ 300 with catabolism, failure of oral agents, pregnancy, acute illness; basal 10 U at night titrated
Evidence: DCCT/EDIC (T1D) and UKPDS (T2D) – tight control ↓ microvascular complications, with legacy effect; DPP: lifestyle prevents T2D
traps: DPP-4 inhibitors do not act on insulin resistance
Metformin dose is NOT started at 2000 mg
GLP-1 RA alone do not cause hypoglycaemia
Only regular insulin is given IV
NPH and premixes are the only cloudy insulins
Basal insulin is used in T2D too
parts: Lecture 3 – Nutrition therapy, insulin, non-insulin drugs, prevention

lectures.title: Overweight, obesity & metabolic syndrome
key: Obesity = abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that impairs health; BMI ≥ 30 (overweight 25–29.9; class I 30–34.9, II 35–39.9, III ≥ 40)
Abdominal (android, visceral) obesity carries the metabolic risk: waist ≥ 80 / 94 cm (IDF Europe) or 88 / 102 cm (ATP III)

Causes: polygenic (FTO, MC4R) + environment (energy-dense food, sedentarity, sleep, stress); secondary – hypothyroidism, Cushing, insulinoma, hypothalamic lesions, PCOS, drugs; monogenic rare (leptin, MC4R)
Complications: T2D, HT, dyslipidaemia, CVD, OSA, NAFLD, gallstones, osteoarthritis, cancers, infertility, depression
Metabolic syndrome: 3 of 5 – waist, TG ≥ 150, low HDL, BP ≥ 130/85, FPG ≥ 100; insulin resistance as common soil
Management: realistic goal −5–10 % in 3–6 months; diet deficit 500–750 kcal/day, physical activity, behaviour therapy; weight regain is frequent
Drugs (BMI ≥ 30 or ≥ 27 + comorbidity): orlistat (lipase inhibitor), liraglutide 3 mg, semaglutide 2.4 mg, tirzepatide, naltrexone-bupropion; sibutramine withdrawn
Bariatric surgery: BMI ≥ 40 or ≥ 35 + comorbidity; sleeve, Roux-en-Y bypass; contraindications – psychiatric instability, alcohol/drug dependence, no follow-up
traps: Orlistat inhibits intestinal LIPASE (not cholesterol absorption)
Urinary cortisol is NOT systematic in obesity
Sleep apnoea is an INDICATION, not a contraindication, for surgery
Fenofibrate is not an anti-obesity drug
BMI 29 = overweight

lectures.title: Hypoglycaemia (non-diabetic), hyperuricaemia & malnutrition
key: Non-diabetic hypoglycaemia: Whipple triad; causes – drugs (insulin, SU, alcohol, quinine), critical illness (liver, kidney, sepsis), cortisol/GH deficiency, insulinoma, non-islet tumours (IGF-2), post-bariatric
Work-up during hypoglycaemia (72-h fast): glucose, insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, SU screen, cortisol
Insulinoma: insulin and C-peptide inappropriately high, neuroglycopenia relieved by food; MEN1; localisation CT/MRI/EUS; surgery, diazoxide
Uric acid = end product of PURINE metabolism; hyperuricaemia > 7 mg/dL (men) / 6 (women); 90 % under-excretion; secondary – CKD, diuretics, alcohol, tumour lysis
Gout in only ~20 %; acute flare – colchicine, NSAID, steroids; urate-lowering (allopurinol, febuxostat) for recurrent flares, tophi, stones; target < 6 mg/dL
Malnutrition: marasmus (energy), kwashiorkor (protein, oedema, low albumin), cachexia (disease-related); BMI < 18.5 / weight loss > 5 % per month or > 10 % per 6 months
Assessment: history, BMI, anthropometry, albumin, prealbumin, transferrin; screening tools NRS-2002, MUST, MNA
Support: increase energy AND protein + vitamins; oral supplements → enteral (gut works) → parenteral; refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia)
traps: Cushing and hyperthyroidism do NOT cause hypoglycaemia
Allopurinol is not given in asymptomatic hyperuricaemia
Uric acid comes from purines, not lipids
Enteral is preferred to parenteral
Catheter infection is a risk of PARENTERAL nutrition
gloss: symptoms + low glucose + relief with glucose
shift of P, K, Mg into cells when feeding resumes
parts: Lecture 5 – Obesity prevention, hypoglycaemia, hyperuricaemia, malnutrition

lectures.title: Cardiovascular risk & dyslipidaemia
key: CV risk factors: age, sex, family history, smoking, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes (major); obesity, sedentarity (predisposing)
Risk estimation: SCORE2 / SCORE2-OP / SCORE2-Diabetes (10-year fatal + non-fatal CVD); diabetics are at least moderate risk
Very high risk: documented ASCVD, diabetes with target-organ damage or ≥ 3 RF or T1D > 20 y, eGFR < 30, SCORE2 high → LDL < 55 mg/dL and −50 %
Atherosclerosis: LDL retention and oxidation → endothelial activation → foam cells → fatty streak → fibrous plaque → vulnerable plaque rupture
Lipid panel: TC, HDL, TG, calculated LDL (Friedewald valid if TG < 400 mg/dL); exclude secondary causes (hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, drugs)
Treatment: lifestyle; statins first (LDL ↓ 30–50+ %), + ezetimibe, + PCSK9 inhibitors (SC); bempedoic acid in statin intolerance
Hypertriglyceridaemia: lifestyle (less alcohol, sugar, fructose), statin if CV risk; TG > 500–880 mg/dL → fibrate, omega-3 (pancreatitis prevention)
Atherogenic dyslipidaemia of T2D: TG ↑, HDL ↓, small dense LDL ↑
traps: PCSK9 inhibitors are injections
Statin intolerance → ezetimibe, not fenofibrate
Statins DO lower triglycerides
Rhabdomyolysis on statins is rare
Friedewald invalid if TG > 400 mg/dL
Obesity is not a "major" independent risk factor
parts: Lab 6 – Dyslipidaemia & CV risk cases (Romanian slides)

lectures.title: Nutrition: healthy diet, nutrients, functional foods
key: Energy: lipids 9 kcal/g, alcohol 7, carbohydrates 4, proteins 4; vitamins and minerals = micronutrients without energy
Healthy distribution: carbohydrates 45–60 % (mostly complex, low GI, fibre 25–30 g/day), proteins 15–20 % (0.8 g/kg), fats 25–35 % (saturated < 10 %, trans < 1 %)
Salt < 5 g/day; added sugars < 10 % of energy; 3 meals ± 1–2 snacks; fruit and vegetables ≥ 400 g/day
Mediterranean diet: vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts, olive oil, fish; moderate dairy/poultry; little red meat – ↓ CV events (PREDIMED)
Glycaemic index: low-GI foods → weight control, satiety, lower CV risk; high-GI → insulin resistance, TG ↑, obesity
Protective factors: unsaturated fatty acids (omega-3 anti-inflammatory), fibre, vitamin D, calcium, potassium; harmful – trans and saturated fats, salt, sugary drinks, processed meat
Functional foods: beneficial effect beyond nutrition – prebiotics, probiotics, phytoestrogens, fibre, fish oil (omega-3), coffee, antioxidants
Energy requirement ≈ 25–30 kcal/kg/day (sedentary) to 35–40 (active); diet history, 24-h recall, food-frequency questionnaire
traps: Lipids are 9 kcal/g, not 4
Fish oil = omega-3 (not omega-6)
Carbohydrates, not proteins, are the main energy source
Wine in the Mediterranean diet is moderate (≤ 1–2 glasses), not 2–3

lectures.title: Labs, clinical cases & exam subjects
key: Clinical case method: glycaemic status → type of diabetes → complications & comorbidities (obesity, HT, dyslipidaemia, CV risk) → targets → lifestyle + drugs → monitoring

Typical exam cases: newly diagnosed T1D with ketosis; obese T2D with metabolic syndrome; T2D + ASCVD needing SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA; insulin titration in T1D; dyslipidaemia with SCORE2 and statin dose; prediabetes in a smoker
Self-monitoring: T1D/MDI ≥ 4 tests per day (fasting, pre-meal, bedtime) or CGM (time in range 70–180 mg/dL > 70 %)
Neuropathy exam: inspection, pulses, ankle reflex, monofilament, 128 Hz tuning fork, ABI 0.9–1.3
traps: Always assess CV risk and complications in every diabetes case
Elderly/frail: looser targets (pre-meal 100–140, HbA1c ≤ 8 %)

Practical exam – subjects recalled by students (French)

sx: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, rapid weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision; may start as DKA
ex: Young, normal/low weight, dehydration, Kussmaul breathing if DKA
lab: Glucose ≥ 200 + symptoms; ketonuria/ketonaemia; C-peptide low; anti-GAD65, IA-2, ICA, ZnT8 +; HbA1c
img: Screen TSH (thyroid autoimmunity), coeliac serology; complications from 5 years after diagnosis
tx: Basal-bolus insulin (0.4–0.5 U/kg/day) or pump/closed loop
Carb counting, self-monitoring/CGM, education, sick-day rules
oth: Honeymoon phase; LADA = slow adult form
paths.def: Autoimmune destruction of β-cells → absolute insulin deficiency.

sx: Often asymptomatic (found on screening); polyuria/polydipsia, infections, pruritus vulvae
ex: Overweight/abdominal obesity, acanthosis nigricans, HT
lab: FPG ≥ 126 ×2, HbA1c ≥ 6.5 %, OGTT ≥ 200; C-peptide normal/high, antibodies negative; lipids, eGFR, UACR, ALT
img: Fundus, foot exam, ECG at diagnosis (complications often present)
tx: Lifestyle + metformin; SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA if ASCVD/HF/CKD; stepwise intensification; insulin when needed
oth: DDx: LADA, MODY, secondary diabetes (Cushing, acromegaly, pancreatitis, steroids)
paths.def: Insulin resistance + progressive β-cell dysfunction (90 % of diabetes).

ex: Risk factors: overweight, family history, HT, PCOS, GDM history, acanthosis
tx: Lifestyle: −7 % weight, 150 min/week activity (DPP −58 %)
Metformin if BMI ≥ 35, < 60 y, previous GDM
oth: Screen all adults ≥ 35 y (ADA) or with risk factors
paths.def: Intermediate hyperglycaemia: IFG, IGT or HbA1c 5.7–6.4 %.

ex: Risk factors: age > 35, BMI > 25–30, previous GDM/macrosomia, family history, PCOS, ethnicity
lab: 1st visit: FPG/HbA1c (overt diabetes if ≥ 126 / ≥ 6.5 %); 24–28 wk 75 g OGTT: ≥ 92 fasting, ≥ 180 at 1 h, ≥ 153 at 2 h (one value)
tx: Diet, activity, self-monitoring; insulin if targets not met (metformin possible)
Re-test 4–12 weeks postpartum (OGTT), then every 1–3 years
cx: Macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, pre-eclampsia; future T2D (~50 %)
oth: Targets: fasting < 95, 1 h < 140, 2 h < 120 mg/dL
paths.def: Hyperglycaemia first recognised in the 2nd–3rd trimester, not overt diabetes.

sx: Mild hyperglycaemia in young non-obese person, 3-generation family history
ex: Normal weight, no ketosis
lab: Antibodies negative, C-peptide preserved; genetic testing (HNF1A, GCK, HNF4A)
tx: GCK: no treatment; HNF1A/HNF4A: low-dose sulfonylurea
Secondary: treat cause
oth: Others: pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis, Cushing, acromegaly, pheochromocytoma, steroids, antipsychotics
paths.def: Monogenic diabetes (autosomal dominant) and secondary diabetes.

sx: Polyuria, thirst, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, drowsiness
ex: Dehydration, Kussmaul breathing, fruity (acetone) breath, tachycardia, hypotension
lab: Glucose > 250, pH < 7.3, HCO₃ < 18, ketones ++, anion gap > 12; K (normal/high but total deficit), Na, creatinine, osmolality
img: ECG (K), search trigger: infection markers, cultures, troponin
tx: 0.9 % NaCl, potassium, IV insulin 0.1 U/kg/h, dextrose when glucose < 250, bicarbonate only if pH < 6.9–7
SC basal-bolus overlap when resolved; education
oth: Triggers: new T1D, missed insulin, infection, MI, SGLT2i (euglycaemic)
paths.def: Absolute insulin deficiency → hyperglycaemia + ketosis + metabolic acidosis.

sx: Days–weeks of polyuria, thirst, weakness, confusion → coma, seizures
ex: Profound dehydration, hypotension, focal neurological signs
lab: Glucose > 600, effective osmolality > 320, pH > 7.3, HCO₃ > 18, ketones minimal
tx: Fluids (≈ 9 L deficit, slower correction), K, low-dose IV insulin after fluids, thromboprophylaxis
oth: Elderly T2D, often inaugural
paths.def: Severe hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality without significant ketosis.

sx: Adrenergic: sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety
Neuroglycopenic: confusion, behaviour/mood change, visual disturbance, seizure, coma
ex: Pale, sweaty, tachycardic; hypertonia, Babinski
lab: Capillary/plasma glucose
img: Review drugs (insulin, SU), meals, exercise, alcohol, renal function
tx: Rule of 15 (15 g sugar, recheck at 15 min)
Unconscious: glucagon IM/SC/nasal, IV glucose 20–30 %
oth: SU-induced: prolonged → observe 24–48 h
paths.def: Glucose < 70 mg/dL (level 1), < 54 (level 2), or needing assistance (level 3).

sx: Asymptomatic until late; blurred vision (macular oedema), floaters (haemorrhage)
ex: Fundus: microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots, IRMA, new vessels
lab: HbA1c, BP, lipids
img: Retinal photography/fundus yearly; OCT for macular oedema; fluorescein angiography
tx: Glycaemic & BP control
PRP laser (severe NPDR/PDR), intravitreal anti-VEGF (DME, PDR), vitrectomy
cx: Vitreous haemorrhage, tractional detachment, neovascular glaucoma
oth: Worsens in pregnancy and with rapid HbA1c drop
paths.def: Microangiopathy of the retina; leading cause of blindness in working-age adults.

ex: BP, oedema
lab: UACR (A2 30–300, A3 > 300 mg/g) on 2 of 3 samples; eGFR (CKD-EPI); K
img: Renal ultrasound if atypical; fundus (retinopathy usually present)
tx: BP < 130/80 with ACEi or ARB (max dose), SGLT2i, finerenone, GLP-1 RA; statin; avoid nephrotoxins
Adjust drugs (metformin < 30 stop)
oth: Atypical: no retinopathy, rapid decline, haematuria → other nephropathy
paths.def: Persistent albuminuria and/or eGFR decline attributable to diabetes.

sx: Numbness, burning, tingling, night pain (stocking-glove); autonomic – dizziness, early satiety, ED
ex: Loss of monofilament/vibration/ankle reflexes, deformities, callus, ulcer; pulses, ABI
lab: HbA1c, B12 (metformin), TSH, creatinine
img: Monofilament 10 g, 128 Hz tuning fork, ABI, X-ray/MRI if osteomyelitis
tx: Glycaemic control, foot care education, footwear
Pain: duloxetine, pregabalin, amitriptyline; alpha-lipoic acid
Ulcer: off-loading, debridement, antibiotics, revascularisation
oth: Wagner 0–5
paths.def: Nerve damage (distal symmetric, autonomic, focal) and its foot consequences.

sx: Often silent ischaemia; angina, claudication, TIA
ex: BP, pulses, bruits, ABI
lab: Lipids, HbA1c, eGFR, UACR
img: ECG yearly, stress testing if symptoms, carotid/leg Doppler
tx: Multifactorial: statin (LDL target by risk), BP < 130/80, antiplatelet in secondary prevention, stop smoking, SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA with CV benefit
oth: Main cause of death in diabetes (×2–4 risk)
paths.def: Accelerated atherosclerosis: coronary, cerebrovascular, peripheral.

lab: eGFR before start and yearly, B12
tx: 500–850 mg with meals, titrate to 2000 (max 3000) mg/day; XR forms
Reduce dose eGFR 30–45, stop < 30; pause for iodinated contrast/surgery
cx: GI upset, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis (rare)
oth: No hypoglycaemia, weight-neutral; UKPDS CV benefit in obese
paths.def: Biguanide, first-line in T2D: ↓ hepatic glucose production, ↑ insulin sensitivity.

lab: HbA1c, weight
tx: GLP-1 RA: liraglutide, semaglutide (SC weekly or oral), dulaglutide, exenatide; first choice if ASCVD/obesity
DPP-4i: sitagliptin, vildagliptin, linagliptin (oral, weight-neutral)
cx: GLP-1 RA: nausea, vomiting, gallstones, pancreatitis (rare); DPP-4i: well tolerated
oth: No hypoglycaemia alone; GLP-1 RA ↓ MACE and weight
paths.def: Enhance the incretin effect: glucose-dependent insulin ↑, glucagon ↓.

lab: eGFR, volume status
tx: Empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin
Indicated in HF and CKD regardless of HbA1c
cx: Genital mycotic infections, UTI, volume depletion, euglycaemic DKA (stop before surgery)
oth: ↓ weight, BP, HF hospitalisation, CKD progression
paths.def: Gliflozins block renal glucose reabsorption (proximal tubule) → glycosuria.

ex: Injection sites: abdomen (fast), arm, thigh/buttock (slow); lipohypertrophy
lab: Self-monitoring / CGM, HbA1c
tx: T1D: basal-bolus or pump
T2D: basal 10 U (0.1–0.2 U/kg) at night, +2 U every 3 days to fasting 80–130 → basal-plus → basal-bolus
oth: Regular insulin only for IV; NPH/premix are cloudy
paths.def: Replacement of basal and prandial insulin.

sx: Dyspnoea, snoring, joint pain, low self-esteem
ex: Weight, height, BMI, waist, BP, acanthosis, striae (exclude Cushing), goitre
lab: FPG/HbA1c, lipids, ALT, uric acid, TSH; cortisol only if clinical suspicion
tx: Lifestyle (deficit 500–750 kcal/day, activity, behaviour)
Drugs: GLP-1 RA, tirzepatide, orlistat
Surgery: BMI ≥ 40 or ≥ 35 + comorbidity
cx: T2D, HT, CVD, OSA, NAFLD, cancer, arthrosis, depression
oth: Weight regain frequent → chronic disease approach
paths.def: BMI ≥ 30 kg/m², abnormal fat accumulation impairing health.

ex: Waist, BP
tx: Lifestyle and weight loss first; treat each component
oth: Common soil: visceral fat, insulin resistance
paths.def: Cluster of insulin-resistance-related CV risk factors (3 of 5).

sx: Neuroglycopenia (fasting, exercise), adrenergic symptoms, weight gain
ex: Usually normal
lab: During hypoglycaemia (72-h fast): insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-OHB, SU screen, cortisol
img: Insulinoma localisation: CT/MRI, EUS, Ga-68 exendin/DOTATATE
tx: Insulinoma: surgical enucleation; diazoxide, somatostatin analogues
Other causes: treat cause (hydrocortisone, stop alcohol…)
oth: Insulin + C-peptide high = insulinoma/SU; insulin high + C-peptide low = exogenous insulin
paths.def: Hypoglycaemia (Whipple triad) in a person without glucose-lowering drugs.

sx: Acute monoarthritis (1st MTP joint – podagra) at night; renal colic
ex: Red, hot, swollen joint; tophi (ear, elbows)
lab: Serum urate (may be normal during flare), creatinine; joint fluid: negatively birefringent needle crystals
tx: Flare: colchicine, NSAID, corticosteroid
Urate-lowering: allopurinol (start low, HLA-B*5801), febuxostat; target < 6 (< 5 if tophi)
Diet: less meat, seafood, beer, fructose
oth: Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is generally not treated with drugs
paths.def: Serum urate > 7 mg/dL (men) / 6 (women).

sx: Weight loss, fatigue, infections, amenorrhoea, poor healing
ex: Low BMI, muscle wasting, oedema (kwashiorkor), dry skin, hair loss
lab: Albumin, prealbumin, transferrin, lymphocytes, electrolytes, P, Mg
tx: Increase energy (30–35 kcal/kg) and protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg), vitamins
Oral supplements → enteral → parenteral
Slow refeeding if severe (thiamine, P)
oth: Risk: hospitalisation, elderly, cancer, digestive diseases, alcohol
paths.def: Insufficient energy and/or protein intake or utilisation.

sx: Asymptomatic; pancreatitis if TG very high
ex: Xanthomas (tendon – FH), xanthelasma, arcus cornealis < 45 y, eruptive xanthomas (TG)
lab: TC, HDL, TG, LDL (Friedewald), non-HDL; TSH, glucose, creatinine, ALT, CK if myalgia
img: SCORE2 risk; carotid plaque on ultrasound, CAC score
tx: Lifestyle; statin → + ezetimibe → + PCSK9i; TG: fibrate, omega-3
oth: Secondary causes: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis, diabetes, alcohol, drugs
paths.def: Abnormal plasma lipids: high LDL, high TG, low HDL (primary or secondary).

ex: BP, BMI, waist, pulses
lab: Lipids, glucose/HbA1c, creatinine, UACR
tx: Targets by category: LDL < 55 (very high), < 70 (high), < 100 (moderate); BP < 130/80; no smoking
oth: Primary vs secondary prevention
paths.def: Estimation of 10-year risk of CV events to set prevention intensity.

ex: BMI, waist
lab: Diet history, 24-h recall, food-frequency questionnaire
tx: Carbs 45–60 %, protein 15–20 %, fat 25–35 %; salt < 5 g; fibre 25–30 g; Mediterranean/DASH pattern
oth: Plate method; low GI; limit alcohol
paths.def: Balanced intake covering needs and preventing NCDs.

questions.exam: Exam R1 July 2023, variant 3 – French section (translated)
questions.q: The diagnosis of diabetes mellitus can be confirmed if:

o.t: Two fasting plasma glucose values are ≥ 126 mg/dL
Fasting plasma glucose is 140 mg/dL and HbA1c is 6.3 %
An asymptomatic patient has a random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL
A patient presents with metabolic acidosis and an emergency glucose of 450 mg/dL
Plasma glucose 2 h after an OGTT with 50 g of glucose is 255 mg/dL

questions.note: Two abnormal results confirm diabetes (same test twice, or two different tests). A hyperglycaemic crisis (ketoacidosis) with glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL is diagnostic on its own. HbA1c 6.3 % is below 6.5 % so the two tests are discordant – repeat the abnormal one. A random glucose ≥ 200 counts only with classic symptoms. The OGTT uses 75 g, not 50 g. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The diagnosis of diabetes mellitus can be confirmed if:

o.t: An asymptomatic patient presents with a random plasma glucose > 255 mg/dL
Fasting plasma glucose is 140 mg/dL and HbA1c is 6.7 %
Plasma glucose 2 h after a 75 g OGTT is 255 mg/dL
Two fasting plasma glucose values are ≥ 126 mg/dL
Fasting plasma glucose is 180 mg/dL and HbA1c is 6.3 %

questions.note: Confirmation needs two abnormal results: two FPG ≥ 126, or two different tests both above threshold (FPG ≥ 126 + HbA1c ≥ 6.5 %). A single abnormal test (one OGTT, or FPG with an HbA1c < 6.5 %) must be repeated; a random value needs classic symptoms. (Translated from the French section.)

also: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)
questions.q: Which criteria confirm the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?

o.t: Specific symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) and a plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL
Two fasting plasma glucose values ≥ 126 mg/dL
Glucose ≥ 140 mg/dL 2 h after 75 g of glucose, confirmed by a second test
HbA1c ≥ 6.5 %, confirmed by a second test
HbA1c ≥ 6.0 %, confirmed by a second test

questions.note: Thresholds: FPG ≥ 126 mg/dL (7 mmol/L), 2-h OGTT ≥ 200 mg/dL, HbA1c ≥ 6.5 %, random ≥ 200 mg/dL with symptoms. 140–199 mg/dL at 2 h = impaired glucose tolerance; HbA1c 5.7–6.4 % = prediabetes. (Translated from the French section.)

Is expressed as a percentage of total haemoglobin
Cannot be used for the diagnosis of diabetes
Reflects the mean glucose over the 2–3 weeks before testing
A value < 8 % indicates good glycaemic control

questions.note: HbA1c reflects the previous 2–3 MONTHS (red cell lifespan), is a diagnostic criterion (≥ 6.5 %) and the usual target is < 7 % (individualised 6.5–8 %). (Translated from the French section.)

Overweight
Arterial hypertension
A family history of cardiovascular disease
Polycystic ovary syndrome

questions.note: Screening risk factors: first-degree relative with T2D, overweight/obesity, sedentarity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia (HDL < 35 mg/dL, TG > 250), PCOS, history of GDM or macrosomia, acanthosis nigricans, personal (not family) CVD, high-risk ethnicity. 2013 variant: "HDL > 35 mg/dL" is not a risk factor. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: People at high risk for type 2 diabetes are those with:

o.t: A family history (parents or siblings) of type 2 diabetes
Breast cancer
Arterial hypotension
Acanthosis nigricans
Polycystic ovary syndrome

questions.note: Acanthosis nigricans and PCOS are markers of insulin resistance. Hypertension (not hypotension) is a risk factor; breast cancer is not. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Check the correct answers:

In type 2 diabetes, insulin is necessary for survival
In type 1 diabetes, ketoacidosis can start spontaneously
Type 2 diabetics usually have normal weight with recent weight loss
Autoantibodies are positive in type 1 diabetes

questions.note: T2D: C-peptide preserved/high, insulin not vital, overweight. T1D: autoimmune (anti-GAD, IA-2, ICA, ZnT8), absolute insulin deficiency, spontaneous ketoacidosis, normal weight with weight loss. 2013 variant: "T2D cannot have chronic complications at onset" is false – they are often present at diagnosis. (Translated from the French section.)

In T1D, normal weight with recent weight loss is usual
If age at diagnosis is < 30 years, T2D must be excluded
Patients with T1D have positive autoantibodies
Chronic complications at the diagnosis of T1D are rare

questions.note: Ketosis-prone T2D exists but is very rare (the corrected copy accepts A). T2D is increasingly seen in young obese people, so age < 30 does not exclude it. T1D is diagnosed early after onset, so chronic complications are rare at diagnosis (unlike T2D). (Translated from the French section.)

The presence of chronic complications at onset/diagnosis points to type 2 diabetes

questions.q: Mechanisms involved in the onset of type 2 diabetes include:

o.t: β-cell dysfunction
Autoimmunity
Increased incretin effect
Increased hepatic glucose production
Increased glucose utilisation in muscle

questions.note: T2D = insulin resistance + progressive β-cell dysfunction; DeFronzo "ominous octet": ↓ insulin secretion, ↑ glucagon, ↑ hepatic glucose output, ↓ muscle uptake, ↑ lipolysis, ↓ incretin effect, ↑ renal glucose reabsorption, brain dysregulation. Autoimmunity = T1D. (Translated from the French section.)

o.t: Deficient glucagon secretion
Increased hepatic glucose production
Increased lipolysis
Decreased renal glucose reabsorption
Decreased incretin effect

questions.note: Glucagon is INCREASED (and insulin deficient); renal reabsorption via SGLT2 is INCREASED – which is why SGLT2 inhibitors work. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In type 2 diabetes, which affirmations about the pathogenetic mechanism are TRUE?

o.t: It involves both β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance
β-cell destruction
At diagnosis, about 50 % of β-cells are dysfunctional
Abdominal obesity leads to insulin resistance
High glucagon secretion

questions.note: UKPDS: at diagnosis ~50 % of β-cell function is lost. Visceral fat releases free fatty acids and adipokines → insulin resistance. Autoimmune β-cell destruction = T1D.

questions.q: Which of the following affirmations are TRUE?

o.t: Diabetes mellitus alters glucose, protein and lipid metabolism
Type 2 diabetes is a metabolic disorder characteristic of adults
Patients with diabetes are at high risk of myocardial infarction
Diabetes is characterised by defects of insulin secretion
Obesity is a monogenic disease

questions.note: Common obesity is polygenic and multifactorial (monogenic forms – MC4R, leptin – are rare).

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes mellitus:

o.t: Results from a progressive defect in insulin secretion due to obesity
Is an autoimmune disease
Results from genetic defects in insulin secretion
Results from β-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency
Occurs more frequently at a young age

questions.note: Genetic defects of insulin secretion = MODY (other specific types). Progressive secretory defect on a background of insulin resistance = T2D.

questions.q: Clinical and paraclinical characteristics of type 1 diabetes:

o.t: Autoantibodies (ICA, anti-GAD) positive, C-peptide high
Young patient, usually normal weight, with recent weight loss
Chronic complications present from onset
Autoantibodies (ICA, anti-GAD) positive, C-peptide low
Patient over 40 years, obese

questions.note: T1D: low/undetectable C-peptide (no endogenous insulin) with positive autoantibodies.

questions.q: Clinical and paraclinical characteristics of type 2 diabetes:

o.t: Chronic complications may already be present at diagnosis
Multiple-dose insulin or a pump must be started from onset
Obese, sedentary person with a family history of T2D
It usually starts with ketoacidosis
Normal or elevated C-peptide and positive autoantibodies

questions.note: T2D: C-peptide normal/high and autoantibodies NEGATIVE; first-line is lifestyle + metformin, not insulin.

questions.q: Characteristics of type 2 diabetes:

o.t: Age at diagnosis mostly under 30 years
C-peptide positive
Hyperketonaemia occurring spontaneously
Ketoacidosis may appear (precipitated by stress/infection)
Usually overweight/obesity at diagnosis

questions.note: Spontaneous ketosis suggests T1D; in T2D ketoacidosis needs a precipitating factor (infection, MI, steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors).

questions.q: Which statements are TRUE?

o.t: In type 2 diabetes, patients are usually overweight or obese
Ketoacidosis occurs spontaneously mainly in type 2 diabetes
Insulin therapy has no effect in type 2 diabetes
Atherogenic dyslipidaemia is more common in type 2 diabetes
Chronic complications are already present at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes

questions.note: Atherogenic dyslipidaemia of insulin resistance: high TG, low HDL, small dense LDL.

questions.q: Individuals at high risk of developing type 2 diabetes:

o.t: Those with obesity and physical inactivity
Women who delivered a baby > 4000 g
Women with more than 3 children
Men over 60 years
First-degree relatives of people with diabetes

questions.note: Age ≥ 45 years is a risk factor for both sexes; parity by itself is not.

questions.q: Screening for gestational diabetes – check the single correct answer:

o.t: Screening is mandatory in all pregnant women
The OGTT methodology in pregnancy is identical to that of adults
It is recommended in the presence of risk factors
In the 1st trimester a 75 g OGTT is recommended
A 100 g OGTT is recommended between 24 and 28 weeks

questions.note: Course key: targeted screening in women at risk (age > 35, BMI > 25–30, previous GDM/macrosomia, family history, PCOS, ethnicity). 1st trimester: fasting glucose/HbA1c to detect overt diabetes; 24–28 weeks: 75 g OGTT (one-step, thresholds 92/180/153 mg/dL – any one value), which differs from the non-pregnant OGTT. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Screening for gestational diabetes should be done:

o.t: In women with pre-pregnancy obesity
In women with type 2 diabetes
At 24–28 weeks of gestation
In all pregnant women at the very beginning of pregnancy
If excessive weight gain occurs in the first months

questions.note: Women with known T2D already have pregestational diabetes – they are not screened for GDM.

questions.q: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are:

o.t: Overweight
Diabetes mellitus
Cardiovascular diseases
Arterial hypertension
Cancers

questions.note: WHO 4 main NCDs: cardiovascular disease, cancer, chronic respiratory disease and diabetes (+ mental health in the 5×5 approach). Overweight and hypertension are RISK FACTORS of NCDs. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis – check the single correct answer:

o.t: Bicarbonate is recommended if pH > 7
Thrombo-embolic complications are caused by the treatment
Rapid insulin is given subcutaneously in the first phase of treatment
Potassium deficit is rare
Glucose is given when glycaemia falls below 2.5 g/L

questions.note: Add 5 % dextrose when glucose falls below ~250 mg/dL (2.5 g/L) to keep insulin running until ketosis clears. Bicarbonate only if pH < 6.9–7. Insulin is IV (continuous) first. Total-body K deficit is ALWAYS present. Cerebral oedema (children) and hypokalaemia/hypoglycaemia are treatment complications; thrombosis is due to dehydration. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis – check the single correct answer:

o.t: Glucose is indicated when glycaemia falls below 5 g/L
Rapid insulin is given intravenously
Potassium deficit is rare
Bicarbonate is recommended if pH > 7
Thrombo-embolic complications are caused by the treatment

questions.note: IV regular/rapid insulin (0.1 U/kg/h) after fluid resuscitation and once K ≥ 3.3 mmol/L. Glucose is added below ~250 mg/dL (2.5 g/L), not 5 g/L. (Translated from the French section.)

also: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)
questions.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis – check the correct answers:

o.t: Glucose administration is contraindicated
Rapid insulin is given subcutaneously in the first phase of treatment
Potassium deficit is rare
Bicarbonate is recommended if pH < 7
Hypoglycaemia is a complication related to treatment

questions.note: Treatment order: 1 rehydration (0.9 % saline 1 L/h), 2 potassium, 3 IV insulin, then dextrose when glucose < 250 mg/dL. SC insulin only after ketosis resolves (overlap 1–2 h). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In an insulin-treated diabetic, which cause should be considered first for a coma of abrupt onset?

o.t: Lactic acidosis
Hyperosmolar state
Hypoglycaemia
Ketoacidosis
Stroke

questions.note: Abrupt coma in an insulin- or sulfonylurea-treated patient = hypoglycaemia until proven otherwise: check capillary glucose and give glucose/glucagon. DKA and HHS develop over hours to days. (Translated from the French section.)

also: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)
questions.q: Which signs help diagnose (diabetic) hypoglycaemia?

o.t: Mood changes
Dehydration
Profuse sweating
Visual disturbances
Kussmaul-type dyspnoea

questions.note: Adrenergic (sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger) and neuroglycopenic (confusion, behaviour/mood change, diplopia/blurred vision, seizures, coma) signs. Dehydration and Kussmaul breathing = ketoacidosis. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which statements are FALSE?

o.t: Hyperglycaemic coma sets in rapidly (minutes)
Hyperglycaemic coma is preceded by polyuria–polydipsia
Systolic hypertension is common in hyperglycaemic coma
Hypoglycaemic coma is profound and calm
Ketonic breath is specific for hyperglycaemic (ketoacidotic) coma

questions.note: Hyperglycaemic coma develops over hours–days with dehydration and HYPOtension. Hypoglycaemic coma is agitated, sweaty, with hypertonia/Babinski, of abrupt onset.

questions.q: About the hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, TRUE statements:

o.t: Seen in the elderly; must be distinguished from ketoacidosis
Usually occurs in type 2 diabetes
Arterial pH > 7.30
Plasma osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg
Severe dehydration

questions.note: HHS: glucose > 600 mg/dL, effective osmolality > 320, pH > 7.30, HCO₃ > 18, little or no ketones, profound dehydration (~9 L), altered consciousness; mortality higher than DKA.

questions.q: The hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic syndrome is characterised by:

o.t: Symptoms of hyperglycaemia: polyuria, intense thirst, polydipsia
Normal plasma osmolarity
Signs and symptoms of dehydration
Ketonuria
Metabolic acidosis

questions.note: Osmolarity is HIGH; ketones and acidosis are absent or minimal (residual insulin blocks lipolysis).

questions.q: Signs and symptoms of severe hyperglycaemia:

o.t: Sweating
Hypertension
Confusion
Weight gain

questions.note: Severe hyperglycaemia: polyuria, thirst, dehydration, weight loss, fatigue, confusion up to coma. Sweating suggests hypoglycaemia.

questions.q: The following situations lead to hyperglycaemia:

o.t: Non-compliance with self-monitoring
Skipping meals while on oral agents or insulin
Interruption of insulin treatment
Presence of an infection

questions.note: Skipping meals under insulin/sulfonylureas causes HYPOglycaemia. Infection raises counter-regulatory hormones → hyperglycaemia ("sick day").

questions.q: Complications specific for diabetes mellitus are:

o.t: Ketoacidosis
Stroke
Hypoglycaemia (treatment-induced)
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic syndrome
Foot ulcer

questions.note: Stroke is a macrovascular complication shared with the general population (not specific).

questions.q: Diagnosis of hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes (Whipple triad) includes:

o.t: Low plasma glucose (< 70 mg/dL)
Disappearance of symptoms after protein-containing food
Disappearance of symptoms after carbohydrates
Polyuria and polydipsia
Symptoms of hypoglycaemia

questions.note: Whipple triad: symptoms + low glucose measured at that time + relief after glucose. Levels: 1 < 70, 2 < 54 mg/dL, 3 = severe (needs help).

also: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)
questions.q: Check the correct answers (chronic complications):

o.t: Diabetic retinopathy is a rare complication of diabetes
Retinopathy surveillance is done by fundus examination every 5 years
Pan-retinal photocoagulation is indicated in all proliferative retinopathies
The last stage of diabetic nephropathy is overt macroalbuminuric nephropathy
Diabetic polyneuropathy is bilateral and symmetric

questions.note: Retinopathy is common (leading cause of blindness in working age), screened every 1–2 years. Nephropathy ends in end-stage kidney disease (dialysis), after overt proteinuria. Distal symmetric "stocking-glove" polyneuropathy is the commonest neuropathy. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Check the correct answers (variant):

o.t: Diabetic retinopathy is a rare complication of diabetes
Retinopathy surveillance is done by fundus examination every 5 years
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are used in all diabetic retinopathies
Overt (patent) nephropathy is defined by albuminuria of 30–300 mg/24 h
Diabetic polyneuropathy is bilateral and symmetric

questions.note: Anti-VEGF is used for diabetic macular oedema and proliferative retinopathy, not mild NPDR. 30–300 mg/24 h = moderately increased albuminuria (A2, "microalbuminuria"); overt nephropathy is > 300 mg/24 h (A3). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.exam: Exam R1 July 2023, variant 3 – French section (translated)

It is repeated every 5 years
Fundus examination screens for diabetic retinopathy
It must start at diagnosis in T2D
In T1D it starts 5 years after diagnosis (or at puberty if diagnosed in childhood)

questions.note: Annual screening: retinopathy (fundus/retinal photo), kidney (UACR AND eGFR), neuropathy/foot (monofilament, vibration, pulses). T2D from diagnosis; T1D after 5 years. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Systematic screening for chronic complications – TRUE statements:

o.t: It must start at diagnosis in T1D
It must start at diagnosis in T2D
It is repeated every 5 years
Chronic kidney disease screening uses only the urinary albumin/creatinine ratio
Fundus examination screens for diabetic retinopathy

questions.note: T1D: from 5 years after diagnosis. Repeat yearly. CKD = UACR + eGFR. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.exam: Exam R1 July 2023, variant 3 – French section (translated)
questions.q: Treatment measures indicated in chronic complications:

o.t: ACE inhibitor or ARB for diabetic retinopathy
Strict glycaemic and blood-pressure control
Alpha-lipoic acid in diabetic neuropathy
Retinal photocoagulation in all forms of diabetic retinopathy
SGLT2 inhibitors in diabetic nephropathy/CKD

questions.note: ACEi/ARB are for nephropathy (albuminuria) and hypertension. Photocoagulation: severe NPDR/proliferative retinopathy, not all forms. Neuropathy: alpha-lipoic acid, benfotiamine, and for pain duloxetine/pregabalin/amitriptyline. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Main manifestations of autonomic neuropathy:

o.t: Resting tachycardia
Foot ulcer
Sweating disorders (hyperhidrosis / gustatory sweating)
Cough
Erectile dysfunction

questions.note: Autonomic: resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, diarrhoea/constipation, neurogenic bladder, erectile dysfunction, sudomotor dysfunction, hypoglycaemia unawareness. Ulcers come from sensory neuropathy ± ischaemia.

questions.q: Pathogenic mechanisms of macro- and microangiopathy include:

o.t: Postprandial hypoglycaemia
Accumulation of advanced glycation end products
Oxidative stress
Low levels of vitamins
Endothelial dysfunction

questions.note: Hyperglycaemia → polyol pathway, AGEs, PKC activation, hexosamine pathway → oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation.

questions.q: Chronic microvascular complications – TRUE statements:

o.t: Numbness, plantar burning and tingling are symptoms of peripheral arterial disease
In T2D, screening is recommended only if symptomatic
Poor glycaemic control and high blood pressure are risk factors for retinopathy
Normal visual acuity means no diabetic retinopathy
In T1D, screening is recommended 5 years after diagnosis

questions.note: Those sensory symptoms are neuropathic; PAD gives claudication. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until late, so visual acuity cannot exclude it.

o.t: The initial dose of metformin is 2000 mg
DPP-4 inhibitors act on insulin resistance
GLP-1 receptor agonists increase satiety
Sulfonylureas are associated with weight gain
Metformin is contraindicated if eGFR < 30 mL/min

questions.note: Metformin: start 500–850 mg once/twice daily with meals, titrate to 2000–3000 mg; reduce if eGFR 30–45, stop < 30. DPP-4 inhibitors raise endogenous GLP-1 → glucose-dependent insulin secretion and ↓ glucagon. Pioglitazone is the insulin sensitiser. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Check the single correct answer:

GLP-1 receptor agonists increase satiety
DPP-4 inhibitors act on insulin resistance
The initial dose of metformin is 2000 mg
Sulfonylureas are not associated with weight gain

questions.note: Metformin contraindication is eGFR < 30 (dose reduction 30–45). GLP-1 RA slow gastric emptying and act centrally → satiety, weight loss. (Translated from the French section.)

also: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)

o.t: Metformin is the first-choice drug for all type 2 diabetics without contraindication
Exenatide is given orally
DPP-4 inhibitors act on insulin resistance
The initial dose of metformin is 2000 mg
Sulfonylureas are not associated with a risk of hypoglycaemia

questions.note: Exenatide is a subcutaneous GLP-1 RA (oral form exists only for semaglutide). Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin independently of glucose → hypoglycaemia and weight gain. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.exam: Exam R1 July 2023, variant 3 – French section (translated)
questions.q: Check the correct answers:

o.t: SGLT2 inhibitors increase glycosuria
GLP-1 receptor agonists are associated with a risk of hypoglycaemia
A disadvantage of thiazolidinediones is the risk of heart failure
Metformin is associated with weight gain
GLP-1 receptor agonists are associated with nausea and vomiting

questions.note: GLP-1 RA act glucose-dependently → no hypoglycaemia alone. Pioglitazone: fluid retention, heart failure, weight gain, fractures. Metformin is weight-neutral or slightly lowers weight. (Translated from the French section.)

o.t: DPP-4 inhibitors
GLP-1 analogues
Insulin
SGLT2 inhibitors
Sulfonylureas

questions.note: Insulin and insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas, glinides) cause hypoglycaemia; incretin-based drugs, SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin and pioglitazone do not when used alone.

questions.q: Which statements are FALSE?

o.t: Insulin therapy is compulsory in type 2 diabetes from the start
In newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes, insulin therapy is compulsory
Metformin is first-line therapy in type 2 diabetes
Insulin is always compulsory in type 2 diabetes, with stepwise dose increase

The recommended injection site for NPH insulin is the abdomen
The basal regimen is reserved for type 1 diabetes
Regular human insulin can be given IV or IM in emergencies
Biphasic (premixed) insulins contain prandial insulin (analogue or human) mixed with NPH

Only regular insulin is used IV. (Translated from the French section.)

The basal regimen is reserved for type 1 diabetes

Prandial insulins are inhomogeneous suspensions
Biphasic insulins are clear solutions

Abdominal obesity: waist ≥ 88 cm (women), ≥ 102 cm (men)

Triglycerides ≥ 150 mg/dL or specific treatment

24-h urinary free cortisol is part of the systematic obesity work-up

Liraglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, is an anti-obesity drug

also: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)

o.t: Orlistat is an intestinal lipase inhibitor
Waist circumference ≥ 80 cm in women indicates abdominal obesity
Fenofibrate is an anti-obesity drug
Hypothyroidism is a secondary cause of obesity
Pancreatic tumours (insulinoma) are secondary causes of obesity

questions.note: Secondary obesity: hypothyroidism, Cushing, insulinoma, hypothalamic lesions, GH deficiency, PCOS, drugs (steroids, antipsychotics, insulin). Fenofibrate is a lipid-lowering drug. 2013 variant: BMI 29 = overweight (obesity ≥ 30); waist > 88 cm in MEN does not define abdominal obesity (94/102). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.exam: Exam April 2013, variant II – French section (translated)

Sibutramine is used in Europe to treat obesity

Overweight cannot be treated with drugs when risk factors are absent
Drugs can be used if BMI ≥ 30 regardless of other risk factors

Nutritional therapy should be adapted to each patient
Weight regain is frequent after weight loss
Obesity is rarely seen in children
Abdominal obesity is associated with high metabolic risk

questions.q: The aetiological work-up of hypoglycaemia (non-diabetic) relies on:

o.t: Uncompensated physical effort in non-diabetics
Cortisol measurement
Insulin and C-peptide measurement
TSH measurement
Looking for an overdose of glucose-lowering drugs

questions.note: During a spontaneous or 72-h fast hypoglycaemia: insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, β-hydroxybutyrate, sulfonylurea screen; cortisol (and GH) for adrenal/pituitary insufficiency. High insulin + high C-peptide = insulinoma or secretagogues; high insulin + low C-peptide = exogenous insulin. (Translated from the French section.)

o.t: Cushing syndrome
Pituitary insufficiency
Insulinoma
Liver failure
Hyperthyroidism

questions.note: Also: adrenal insufficiency, alcohol, drugs (quinine, pentamidine), sepsis, renal failure, non-islet cell tumours (IGF-2), post-bariatric hypoglycaemia. Cushing causes hyperglycaemia. (Translated from the French section.)

o.t: Gout is present in 80 % of hyperuricaemias
The risk of kidney stones is low
All asymptomatic hyperuricaemias must be treated with allopurinol
Allopurinol has good digestive tolerance
Chronic kidney disease is a secondary cause of hyperuricaemia

Uric acid is the final product of lipid metabolism
~70 % of daily urate is excreted by the kidneys, the rest by the gut

Normal uric acid in women is below 6 mg/dL

questions.q: Management of malnutrition should include:

o.t: Decreased nitrogen (protein) intake
Increased caloric intake
Artificial nutrition if there are digestive losses
Multivitamins
Preference for the parenteral route if artificial nutrition is needed

questions.note: Increase calories AND protein, add vitamins/minerals; if artificial nutrition is needed, the enteral route is preferred whenever the gut works ("if the gut works, use it"). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which statements about malnutrition are TRUE?

o.t: Artificial feeding is recommended if the oral route is available
A risk of enteral feeding is catheter infection
Albumin and prealbumin are part of the malnutrition work-up
BMI < 15 kg/m² is an indication for parenteral nutrition
Hospitalisation is a risk factor

questions.note: Catheter infection is a risk of PARENTERAL nutrition. BMI < 15 = very severe (grade 3) malnutrition with mucosal atrophy – parenteral support is accepted. Hospitalisation is both a risk factor and a setting where malnutrition is detected (student keys differ on E). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Malnutrition – TRUE with ONE EXCEPTION (choose the false one):

o.t: Cachexia: weight loss > 5 %, or BMI < 20 with weight loss > 2 %, or sarcopenia with weight loss > 2 %
In kwashiorkor, a smaller weight loss can be masked by oedema
Kwashiorkor is protein malnutrition with negative nitrogen balance
Marasmus is a catabolic state unresponsive to treatment, with survival < 3 months
Marasmus is energy malnutrition (negative energy balance)

questions.note: "Unresponsive, survival < 3 months" defines refractory cachexia, not marasmus. Marasmus = global energy deficit with muscle/fat wasting, no oedema, albumin near normal.

o.t: LDL-cholesterol target in the moderate-risk category is < 70 mg/dL

questions.note: ESC targets: moderate risk LDL < 100 mg/dL, high < 70 (and ≥ 50 % reduction), very high < 55. Only some GLP-1 RA proved CV benefit (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide). SGLT2i are given in HF regardless of HbA1c. (Translated from the French section.)

Reduced cardiovascular risk

Proteins should provide 15–20 % of total energy
Lipids should provide only 10 % of energy because of atherogenic risk
Trans fatty acids should be < 1 % of energy
A junk-food diet is associated with cardiovascular disease and obesity

questions.note: Healthy distribution: carbohydrates 45–60 %, proteins 15–20 %, lipids 25–35 % (saturated < 10 %, trans < 1 %).

Omega-3 fatty acids are pro-inflammatory
Unsaturated fats decrease total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides
Dietary fibres are considered functional foods
In obesity the diet should be < 1000 kcal/day

questions.note: Omega-3 are anti-inflammatory. Usual weight-loss diet: deficit of 500–750 kcal/day (≈ 1200–1500 kcal women, 1500–1800 men); very-low-calorie diets only under supervision.

questions.q: Which statements are FALSE?

Lipids and carbohydrates are energy-providing macronutrients
Proteins are the main source of energy
A healthy diet has 3 meals and 1–2 snacks per day
Moderate alcohol intake may have benefits in healthy people

questions.note: Vitamins are micronutrients without energy; carbohydrates are the main energy source. Note: recent guidance says there is no safe level of alcohol, but the course statement E is accepted as true.
